lesson.menu_title: Numbers That Tell a Story -- Presenting Data and Scale
lesson.menu_desc: Present the numbers behind Sebrae-SP and the geographic indication program to an Italian partner, with approximation language like 'approximately', 'nearly' and 'more than' -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 -- Numbers That Tell a Story
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávia Florêncio Ferreira | Lesson 21 -- Numbers That Tell a Story
lesson.grammar_point: approximation language for numbers and data (approximately, nearly, over, more than)

listenings.text: Hello, Flavia. This is Luca Bianchi, from the chamber of commerce in Parma. Thank you for your email about the mission. Before our meeting on Thursday, I have a request. Our members love numbers. Please bring three or four figures about your program. For example, how many producers do you support? What percentage of them sell outside Brazil? And what is the growth of the program in the last three years? You do not need exact numbers. Approximately is fine. Our team will prepare a short report for our members. See you on Thursday.

Here is a simple tip for presenting numbers. Do not read a long list of figures. People forget them very fast. Choose only three numbers, and give each number a meaning. For example, do not say twelve thousand four hundred and eighty producers. Say more than twelve thousand producers. It is shorter, and people remember it. Then, compare the number with something they know: that is nearly the population of a small town. Finally, end with the trend. Is the number growing or falling? A number with a story is a number people remember.

extra_audio.text: First, I choose three important figures about the program. Then, I round each number, like more than twelve thousand producers. Next, I open with a framing phrase: to give you an idea of the scale. After that, I compare the number with something my partner knows. Finally, I end with the trend, and I say the program is growing.
